title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment (N = 300 matched intents) to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations from an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. The run used a shared_initial_candidate generation contract (one LLM candidate replayed to both arms), declared model gpt-5-mini, two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, and a preregistered repair policy allowing up to one repair call when a validator detects forbidden reachability. Results were degenerate: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (paired contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% CI for paired risk-difference = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Because validators never reported forbidden reachability, no repair calls were invoked and the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis about repair efficacy was untestable under this run (shared replay semantics + zero observed violations). As a descriptive bound, the one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on a baseline violation rate is ≈0.00994. We release machine-readable preregistration, per-episode validator traces, provider-call accounting (model_calls_used = 300), responses, and analysis artifacts to enable reproducible follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise the repair path (independent draws, stronger adversaries, multi-model comparisons).

sections.introduction:
LLMs promise to automate intent-driven network configuration, but operational risk remains: generated artifacts can introduce security-relevant regressions (for example, expanding reachability to protected management interfaces). Prior systems and surveys therefore advocate execution oracles, constrained generation, and iterative generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as mitigations [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898; https://openalex.org/W4415071524]. Motivated by an evidence gap—preregistered, deterministic evaluations that quantify whether a verifier placed in the loop reduces forbidden-reachability misconfigurations under adversarial inputs—we designed and executed a confirmatory paired experiment.

Research question (final, preregistered): Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline?  
Contributions: (1) a machine-readable preregistration fixing a paired N = 300 confirmatory design; (2) a deterministic Dockerized execution under a shared_initial_candidate contract (one initial LLM candidate per paired intent) with provider-call accounting (model_calls_used = 300); (3) fully archived per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis artifacts showing a degenerate confirmatory result (no validator-detected violations; repair never invoked) together with descriptive statistical bounds; (4) concrete, artifact-grounded design lessons and reproducibility materials to guide follow-up stress tests that exercise the repair path. Importantly, because no validator-detected violations occurred, the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis about repair efficacy is untestable in this run; we state this unambiguously and quantify descriptive bounds on undetected violation rates.
sections.related_work:
Three literatures frame the study. First, generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures have improved correctness on code and IaC tasks by using verifier feedback to guide repair; realized gains depend strongly on verifier power and repair strategy (e.g., TerraFormer and related verifier-feedback systems) [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898]. Second, surveys and NetOps system papers document LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch) and recommend validators, constrained generation, or human oversight for operational safety [https://openalex.org/W4415071524; https://openalex.org/W4404602270]. Third, emulation and testbed work shows execution-based validation is feasible for research-grade evaluation but highlights external-validity limits when porting to production networks [https://openalex.org/W4406170828].

Prior work motivates verifier-in-the-loop designs but does not provide a preregistered, deterministic paired evaluation that (a) fixes generation semantics explicitly, (b) archives per-episode validator traces for audit, and (c) quantifies compute/accounting trade-offs under a fixed model-call budget—gaps our experiment was designed to address.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered as cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1. Confirmatory design: paired binary design with N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds + 150 programmatic adversarial variants). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Confirmatory test: exact McNemar two-sided test (alpha = 0.05). Prespecified CI method: bootstrap percentile; final analysis used 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729), recorded in the analysis log.

Generation semantics and adapter contract: To limit provider usage the preregistration specified a shared_initial_candidate contract: a single initial LLM candidate was generated per paired intent and replayed to both arms (baseline and guarded). This choice produced model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs (execution manifest records model_calls_used = 300 and 'shared_initial_generation' = 300). Because baseline replays the shared candidate rather than drawing an independent sample, baseline is not an independent-generation arm and between-arm independent-sample variability is reduced—a design choice with inferential consequences (see Results & Discussion).

Intervention arms and repair policy: Baseline = the shared initial candidate replayed directly. Guarded = the same initial candidate validated by deterministic validators; if a validator reports forbidden reachability the preregistered policy allowed up to one repair LLM call. Repair calls were to be logged and counted; across this run no repair calls were invoked because validators never reported forbidden reachability.

Validators and forbidden-reachability predicate (concise technical definition): Two deterministic validators were used and combined with a logical-OR decision rule: a pair is labeled 'violating' if any validator reports the forbidden-reachability predicate. The validators are recorded per episode as validator_id = 'deterministic_netops_validator_v5' (validator_version = '5.0'); per-episode validator_trace artifacts implement the concrete predicate checks used in scoring. In plain terms the forbidden-reachability predicate corresponds to validator-detected violations of the run's policy/profile constraints (reachability or policy conditions that the test tasks mark as forbidden, including protection of designated management interfaces and workflow-policies encoded in each task). The exact algorithmic checks, ACL/route-policy semantics included, and normalization rules are archived in the per-episode validator_trace records (execution/scoring/*.json) and are the authoritative specification for the predicate and each validator's detection model. We summarize here only that (a) both validators operate deterministically under the Dockerized emulator, (b) their outputs were combined by logical OR (any positive -> violating), and (c) repair was invoked only on validator-detected violations.

Execution and reproducibility backbone: The environment used Dockerized FRRouting-style router images, deterministic orchestration, and programmatic task generation; per-episode raw responses, provider-call audit, execution manifest, task manifest, and scoring traces are archived (representative files: execution/raw_results.jsonl; execution/responses/; execution/scoring/*.json; execution/execution_manifest.json; analysis/*). These artifacts permit deterministic replay under the same adapter contract.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions); completed episodes = 600; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 300 (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Confirmatory outcomes: baseline_success_count = 300; guarded_success_count = 300. Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. McNemar exact two-sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the paired risk-difference (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Because no validator-detected violations occurred, the repair path was never invoked (per-episode validator_trace.repair_applied = false in scoring artifacts) and verifier_disagreement_rate = 0 across archived validator outputs.

Interpretation of numeric results: The paired test is uninformative about repair efficacy when no discordant pairs exist—here, shared replay semantics combined with zero observed validator-detected violations produced a degenerate contingency (no events for McNemar to compare). As a descriptive bound, observing 0/300 violations gives a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the (undetected) baseline violation rate of approximately 1 - 0.05^(1/300) ≈ 0.00994 (~0.994%). Representative archived artifacts (e.g., execution/responses/task-000001-*.txt and execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json) illustrate typical medium-difficulty tasks where the shared candidate passed both validators.
sections.discussion:
Primary-inference outcome and untestability: The preregistered primary hypothesis concerned whether verifier-in-the-loop repair reduces forbidden-reachability misconfigurations. That hypothesis required (a) observable initial violations and (b) repair activity to be invoked on at least some discordant pairs. In this run both conditions failed to produce any validator-detected violations; consequently the preregistered confirmatory test about repair efficacy is untestable here. We state this explicitly: the experiment demonstrates that, under the chosen model (declared gpt-5-mini), validators, emulator, task set, and shared_initial_candidate contract, baseline generation satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate for all sampled intents; it does not show that verifiers are unnecessary or that repair cannot rescue violations under other designs.

Design lessons and operational implications (artifact-grounded): (1) Generation semantics matter: shared_initial_candidate reduces model calls (model_calls_used = 300) but also reduces independent-sample variability needed to produce discordant pairs that repair could fix. For demonstration of repair efficacy, independent-condition generation (two independent LLM draws per pair) or larger sample sizes are recommended. (2) Adversary potency matters: programmatic adversarial variants used here did not trigger validator-detectable forbidden reachability for this model/validator configuration; targeted or stronger adversaries should be used to exercise repair paths. (3) Verifier strength/diversity matters: two deterministic validators combined by OR produced perfect concordance in this run; including richer oracles or production-grade validators could change detection dynamics. (4) Reproducible accounting is practical: per-episode traces, provider-call audit, and archived analysis logs permit exact verification of the run's deterministic accounting and statistical summaries.

Threats to validity (concise): Internal validity: reduced by shared replay semantics limiting independent draws; no technical failures occurred. Construct validity: depends on whether the archived forbidden-reachability predicate and the two validators capture operationally meaningful security risk; the authoritative predicate and validator behavior are in the per-episode validator_trace artifacts. External validity: synthetic tasks and Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation limit transportability to heterogeneous production devices and live-traffic conditions. Conclusion validity: the degenerate contingency violates preregistered power assumptions and renders confirmatory inference about repair efficacy moot. All artifacts and their locations are archived for reanalysis and targeted follow-up tests.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, deterministic paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation. Under the chosen adapter contract (shared_initial_candidate), declared model (gpt-5-mini), two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, and the provided synthetic adversarial perturbations, baseline and guarded arms both passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all N = 300 matched pairs; no validator-detected violations occurred and no repair calls were invoked. Consequently, the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis about verifier-guided repair efficacy is untestable in this run. The primary empirical contribution is deterministic execution accounting, archival of per-episode validator traces and provider-call logs (model_calls_used = 300), and concrete design lessons for follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise the repair path (independent draws, stronger adversaries, multi-model and multi-oracle comparisons). We release the preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis artifacts to enable reproducible follow-up experiments and targeted investigations into verifier-guided repair efficacy.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.

Model and verifier scope: a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
